doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Making a living, teaching himself bass, and getting sober
summary: Tate describes his working life, self-taught bass, and alcohol until 1973 after which things improved.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: What’s it like in this particular time period to make a living as a jazz musician?

I have a wife with a real job so it’s not too bad. My wife works for Doubleday Books, she’s the — well her title I guess it’s the Director of Promotional Art. But I mean she works and I stay busy. I’ve always worked. I knew going in that I wasn’t going to make any money money. I make a living and I work. And it’s two hours a day. I get my golf in by day and I’m not into 60 hour weeks. My father did that and lived to the ripe old age of 61. Forget it. I’m very happy and I’m very, very happy when I think about my circumstance. Because I came at it from a very funny angle. I had no education in music as a kid except trumpet lessons, and I didn’t have any formal education on string bass. I watched bass players. I figured — I got a hold of the Simandl book, then I had a couple of teachers and got the bend out of my wrist and got my arm straightened out and my fingering. And I watched good bass players and watched how they played. And why they held their body a certain way and it started making sense. You know if your wrist is cocked it’s like a support beam with a bend in it. This makes more sense than this, and things like that. And this makes more sense than this. This is stronger and I started figuring it out. And I mostly relied on my ear. And so the point was, and I was 27 before I started playing full time. And had a serious battle with alcohol that lasted from the time I was 16 until I was 30. And it wasn’t really until, when I went on the wagon in 1973, within six months I was out of Washington and off working with Hackett and then McKenna and Marian McPartland, so when I dried out everything good started happening to me at once. And so coming at it from the angle that I came at I sort of crashed the party, and sort of late in life too, I mean, to have made it in this business. It still surprises me when I think about it that I’m doing what I want to do in New York, and it’s what I’ve been doing for 30 years, the same thing. I don’t teach, I don’t write, I didn’t ever want to do any of that, all I ever wanted to do was be a bass player and a performer, and that’s exactly what has happened. So I caught a big break.
